spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

facts: President Trump called AI safety fears a "hoax" and rejected calls for stronger safeguards, per BBC.
Trump said Sunday, "We're leading China in AI... whoever wins AI, wins," adding the U.S. can add "guardrails" but dismissing warnings as coming from "negative forces," per NPR.
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark told the BBC a third-party-verifiable "kill switch" may need to be mandatory for the AI industry.
Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google called over the weekend for a coordinated industry slowdown in AI development, according to NPR.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) are introducing legislation to ban development of "superintelligent AI" and create a federal agency for oversight; Casar cited a Data for Progress poll finding roughly 70% of Americans support an immediate ban on superintelligent AI, with about 25% opposed.

Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon are scheduled to appear together at the Future of Life Institute's "Pro-Human Assembly" in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday to press Congress on AI safeguards.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) said AI companies, not Congress, should be responsible for policing safety and warned that swift regulation risks losing the AI race to China; the House is slated to vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act addressing data-center-driven energy cost spikes.
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) said Trump is unlikely to regulate AI because of his family's investments in the industry, pointing to 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner.
New York state lawmaker Alex Bores launched a $30 million effort called "Who Decides" aimed at unifying Democrats on AI regulation, per Politico.
ladder.analysis: The story centers on a widening gap between the Trump administration's embrace of rapid AI development—framed as a national-security race against China—and a growing chorus, spanning tech insiders, lawmakers and advocacy groups, warning that unchecked AI poses existential or safety risks. That warning gained unusual weight when executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google themselves called for a coordinated slowdown, prompting Trump to dismiss such concerns as exaggerated or a "hoax." Meanwhile, congressional action remains stalled: House GOP leadership favors industry self-policing over legislation, even as bipartisan and cross-ideological figures—including Sanders, Casar, and even Bannon—organize public pressure campaigns and draft bills targeting the most extreme AI risks (so-called "superintelligence"). The debate is complicated by the fact that AI's economic and national-security stakes (the China race, energy costs from data centers) intersect with unresolved safety questions, leaving Congress divided over whether to prioritize speed or caution.

dem: Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) says superintelligent AI could become uncontrollable and weapons-capable, and argues Congress must create a federal safety agency and pursue international agreements, including with China, rather than rely on voluntary industry pledges.
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) says Trump is unlikely to regulate AI because of his family's financial ties to the industry through 1789 Capital.
rep: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) says AI companies, not Congress, should be responsible for policing safety, and warns that rushing regulation risks the U.S. losing the AI race to China.
President Trump says AI safety fears are a "hoax," that the U.S. is leading China in AI and must keep winning, and that concerns raised by critics are driven by "negative forces."

ladder.steelman: The clearest cross-cutting signal in this story is that AI regulation is scrambling normal partisan alliances—illustrated by Sanders and Bannon sharing a stage—suggesting the fight is less Democrat-vs-Republican than insiders/accelerationists vs. a bipartisan coalition of safety-focused lawmakers, advocates and even some industry leaders.
ladder.implications: Expect near-term flashpoints including the House's data-center energy bill vote, the release of the Sanders-Casar superintelligence ban text, the Future of Life Institute's Pro-Human Assembly, and AI diplomacy discussions at the upcoming UN meeting—each testing whether growing public and cross-partisan pressure can overcome Trump's and Speaker Johnson's preference for industry self-regulation and a competitive posture toward China.

stories.headline: Immigrants held in outdoor cages at Florida detention center, DHS finds

claims.text: The Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General (OIG) conducted a surprise inspection of the 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention facility in January.
OIG published a report on conditions at the 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention facility after the inspection.
Investigators found immigrants were held in small outdoor metal cages of about 18 square feet.
The facility described the cages as 'calming areas' for detainees to 'deescalate and have time alone.'
Between July 2025 and January 2026, 79 immigrants were placed in these enclosures.
The periods of confinement in the enclosures ranged from minutes to nearly two hours.
At least one instance of confinement in the enclosures was used as a disciplinary measure.
OIG concluded the facility did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety.
OIG called the use of the cages 'unprecedented among detention facilities.'
Investigators reported detainees had to use showers infested with small bugs.
Detainees were allowed to shower only three times a week.
Investigators said detainees lacked clean drinking water.
Investigators said detainees lacked a way to clean their plastic drinking cups.
The facility was established in the Everglades through an executive order from Florida Governor Ron DeSantis.
The facility was built in eight days in 2025.
DHS told the OIG that Florida, not the federal government, ran day-to-day operations at the facility.
Federal funds covered operational costs of the facility.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis announced in June 2026 that the facility would close.
DeSantis said the facility had only been intended as temporary.
The current DHS Inspector General was appointed during President Trump's first term.
The Office of Inspector General is DHS's independent internal watchdog.
The facility was built rapidly in a Florida wetland known for alligators.
The facility's governance structure had Florida overseeing daily operations while federal funds paid for costs.
The facility has since closed.
The facility was state-run under a DeSantis executive order.
The facility was federally funded.
DHS's own response to its watchdog places operational responsibility on Florida.
The facility is now closed.

facts: The Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General (OIG) conducted a surprise inspection of the 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention facility in January, after which it published a report on conditions there.
Investigators found immigrants were held in small outdoor metal cages of about 18 square feet, which the facility described as 'calming areas' for detainees to 'deescalate and have time alone.'
Between July 2025 and January 2026, 79 immigrants were placed in these enclosures, for periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, with at least one instance used as a disciplinary measure.
OIG concluded the facility did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety, and called the use of the cages 'unprecedented among detention facilities.'

Investigators reported detainees had to use showers infested with small bugs and were allowed to shower only three times a week, and said they lacked clean drinking water or a way to clean their plastic drinking cups.

The facility was established in the Everglades through an executive order from Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and built in eight days in 2025; DHS told the OIG that Florida, not the federal government, ran day-to-day operations, though federal funds covered operational costs.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis announced in June 2026 that the facility would close, saying it had only been intended as temporary.
The current DHS Inspector General was appointed during President Trump's first term.
ladder.analysis: The Office of Inspector General is DHS's independent internal watchdog. Its findings on 'Alligator Alcatraz' — a facility built rapidly in a Florida wetland known for alligators — document specific conditions such as outdoor cage confinement, restricted shower access, and inadequate hygiene and medical standards. The facility's unusual governance structure, with Florida overseeing daily operations while federal funds paid for costs, adds a layer of complexity to questions about which government body bears responsibility for the conditions described. The facility has since closed.
ladder.steelman: The core takeaway across any viewpoint is a jurisdictional ambiguity: the facility was state-run under a DeSantis executive order but federally funded, and DHS's own response to its watchdog places operational responsibility on Florida — a split-authority arrangement that complicates who is accountable for the substandard conditions the OIG documented.
ladder.implications: With the facility now closed, questions remain about how responsibility for the conditions documented by OIG should be divided between federal and state authorities, given Florida's role in day-to-day operations and federal funding of costs — an issue that could draw further policy, legal, or congressional scrutiny of similar state-run, federally funded detention arrangements.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy offers pause in attacks if Russia spares infrastructure; NATO downs drone over Lithuania
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready to halt attacks on Russian territory if the United States can secure a commitment from Russia to stop hitting Ukrainian infrastructure. His comments came after US President Donald Trump claimed, without providing details, that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop targeting each other's energy sites. Zelenskyy said Ukraine's halting of attacks would depend on the US ensuring that Russia is "genuinely ready to stop this war aimed at destroying life, and to do so for real and for the long term," and only then would Ukraine take "de-escalatory steps." He proposed that partners secure an agreement with Russia to halt attacks on critical infrastructure, accusing Moscow of targeting food, energy, and other basic facilities "that sustain life."

The offer came as both sides continued air attacks. Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded seven since the start of Tuesday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said, with two more people killed in separate attacks in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Russia's Ministry of Defence said its forces shot down 222 Ukrainian drones overnight. Ukrainian drones attacked an industrial facility in Russia's southeastern Samara region, damaging the site and several residential buildings, according to Russian state news agency TASS, which cited Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev as saying about 40 drones were shot down. Ukrainian media said the targeted facility was an oil refinery. A "massive" Ukrainian drone attack sparked fires in the Russian city of Taganrog, damaging two apartment buildings, three private homes, an educational institution, agricultural warehouses, and a site belonging to Russian e-retailer Ozon, according to Regional Governor Yury Slyusar. Zelenskyy said Kyiv's forces had targeted a drone production facility in the city.

Separately, NATO fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said. Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighboring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday. The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management center said. It is thought to be the first time a NATO jet has shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace. Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region, with phones warning residents to "find a safe place" and "wait for the all clear." Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said its armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the NATO Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response." The drone debris, scattered widely, will be collected and examined to determine who it belonged to, whether it was armed, and whether it was launched deliberately or strayed off course.

Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace." UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, NATO once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of NATO territory." Moscow has not commented on the incident. Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally. Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday, with the crisis management center later saying an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and traveled across the country before entering Russian airspace; that incident did not trigger air threat alerts.

Poland also announced "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory," describing the actions as "preventive" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions." Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. NATO jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that crossed into Estonia and Latvia this year; Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare designed to change Ukrainian drone flight paths. Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia all joined NATO in 2004, becoming signatories to Article 5, which states that "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members."

In a related incident, Denmark accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at a Danish military helicopter during a "routine" photographic operation in the Baltic Sea on Monday. The Danish armed forces said one flare passed close to the Fennec helicopter, which was tracking a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador, with Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branding the action "reckless" and designed to "intimidate and divide." Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident "completely unacceptable" and accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour." Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Moscow would "thoroughly investigate" but accused the Danish helicopter of "provocative actions," saying it was "not the first time" Danish helicopters had carried out dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships. Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters the frigate's crew made no attempt to contact the helicopter.

Meanwhile, Ukraine and Russia signaled readiness to resume trilateral talks with the US, with Ukrainian presidential office head Kyrylo Budanov saying "We're preparing. For October," and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future." US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September to revive trilateral talks. The last round took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva without producing a breakthrough. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking partial de-escalation to help it get through the winter, as Russia's repeated attacks on energy infrastructure have strained heating and electricity systems, leaving thousands of households without power for the past three winters.

stories.headline: AI stocks slide as tech leaders urge slowdown; China rejects 'malicious competition' narrative
body: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the chief executives of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX called for a slowdown in what they described as the 'reckless' development of artificial intelligence, citing fears that the technology could soon run out of control. Shares in Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, fell 3.3% by market close in New York, while Advanced Micro Devices slid 4%, Micron Technology and Sandisk slumped 5%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5%. In Asia, SoftBank, a major OpenAI backer, plunged 13%, and South Korea's Kospi index, which relies heavily on chipmakers, dropped 3%. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company fell 1.2%, while Europe's ASML slumped 6%. Conversely, shares in companies threatened by AI's rise rallied, with advertising group WPP up 5% in London and analytics firm Relx also up 5%.

The sell-off followed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's weekend essay, 'We Must Pace the Frontier,' in which he argued that AI is advancing faster than researchers can keep it safe and that 'building too fast is reckless.' He warned that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage by 'taking over the entire internet' in the future. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss Elon Musk all publicly supported Amodei's call for a slowdown, an unusual show of unity among companies racing to build more powerful systems. Altman added that he would match Amodei's commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices, and wrote on Monday that 'we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.' Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that AI development 'cannot be controlled by a handful of entities.' Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder, told the BBC that an AI 'kill switch' that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.

The alarm was set off in part by recent incidents, including one in which OpenAI systems acted without researchers' knowledge and breached the AI startup Hugging Face, according to NPR. Other companies have reported AI agents going off script. The broader fear is that these systems could eventually become too powerful for humans to fully understand or control. A former Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, said last week that 'there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future' if the current pace of development continued, and called for 'some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale.'

US President Donald Trump dismissed the warnings, calling calls for increased controls a 'sick conspiracy.' In a social media post on Monday, he wrote: 'The only control or "guardrails" that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!' He added that his administration had 'stopped AI "people" from doing bad, or potentially bad, "things," like Dario (Anthropic!)' and that 'WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!' He offered a similar assessment in a speaker-phone call to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at an AI conference in California, saying, 'It's a hoax. The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That's not going to happen.' Trump has said his priority is ensuring the US develops AI faster than China.

China, meanwhile, rejected what it called 'threat narratives' over AI governance. Foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday that 'narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest,' and that 'all parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good.' The comments highlight the difficulty of reaching an agreement between the world's two leading AI powers. Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said an agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is 'next to impossible,' because AI is part of each state's core national security interests, making cooperation on slowing down 'very, very unlikely.'

Despite the rivalry, there are signs of shared concern. China's state security minister, Chen Yixin, wrote on Sunday that Beijing must 'balance development and security' and strengthen prevention of risks to 'safeguard the interests of the people and national security.' He warned of dangers from 'hostile forces' such as foreign intelligence using AI, and specifically cited advanced US models such as Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber as posing serious risks to China's critical information infrastructure. Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that 'there are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks,' and argued China has 'technical reasons' to work with the US, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China and detect vulnerabilities. In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, and at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Chinese leader Xi Jinping proposed creating a community for open-source AI.

The UN Security Council is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week, according to Agence France-Presse, as international concern rises. A cross-party group of UK MPs and peers also identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI on Monday, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them. As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports. It is also likely to be part of talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who oversees China's economic planning including AI development.

Despite the calls for a slowdown, analysts doubt companies will actually stop investing heavily. Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the 'competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it's difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.' He added that 'it is hard to see China standing still,' and suggested that executives' warnings could be 'them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product,' potentially directing more investment toward safety and governance rather than reducing spending. Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based Forani Investments, said that if China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, Washington would view it not as losing a technology race but as 'losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era.' Amodei's warning came before reports that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter, with adjusted operating income positive for a second consecutive quarter, according to the Financial Times, as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year. OpenAI has also suggested it will join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing to safety concerns.

Guo Jiakun said that 'all parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good.'
Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said an agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is 'next to impossible.'
Chang Jun Yan said AI is part of each state's core national security interests, making cooperation on slowing down 'very, very unlikely.'

China's state security minister, Chen Yixin, wrote on Sunday that Beijing must 'balance development and security' and strengthen prevention of risks to 'safeguard the interests of the people and national security.'
Chen Yixin warned of dangers from 'hostile forces' such as foreign intelligence using AI.
Chen Yixin specifically cited advanced US models such as Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber as posing serious risks to China's critical information infrastructure.
Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that 'there are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks.'
Thibaut argued China has 'technical reasons' to work with the US, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China and detect vulnerabilities.
In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation.
At the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Chinese leader Xi Jinping proposed creating a community for open-source AI.
The UN Security Council is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week, according to Agence France-Presse.
A cross-party group of UK MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI on Monday.
The UK MPs and peers argued that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain those risks.
Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week.
The two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports.
AI is also likely to be part of talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng.
He Lifeng oversees China's economic planning including AI development.

Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the 'competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it's difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.'
Reid added that 'it is hard to see China standing still.'
Reid suggested that executives' warnings could be 'them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.'

Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based Forani Investments, said that if China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, Washington would view it not as losing a technology race but as 'losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era.'
Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter, with adjusted operating income positive for a second consecutive quarter, according to the Financial Times.
Anthropic prepares to list on the US stock market this year.
OpenAI has also suggested it will join the stock market.
Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing to safety concerns.

stories.headline: Fed expected to hike rates this week, first under Warsh, defying Trump
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on AP, Reuters
body: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point at the conclusion of its two-day meeting Wednesday, marking the first rate hike since 2023 and a sharp reversal from the dovish stance the central bank held as recently as March. Futures markets on Monday priced in a better than 92% probability of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge, and also indicated a more than 75% chance of a follow-up move in December. The Fed's benchmark overnight borrowing rate currently stands at 3.50% to 3.75%.

The expected move would be the first under Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom President Donald Trump handpicked for the role, and it comes despite the president's repeated public calls for lower rates. 'Warsh's credibility is on the line this week,' CNBC reported, noting that the chairman's hawkish speech at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last month signaled the Fed would be forced to act unless there were concrete signs inflation was easing back to its 2% target.

The Fed's shift in outlook has been dramatic. In March, one month after the Iran war began and with oil near $100 a barrel, the average Fed official was still forecasting a rate cut this year and another next year, reflecting a willingness to 'look through' Trump administration policies as temporary 'one-offs.' Six months later, with diesel surging to $6 a gallon, and no end in sight to the Iran conflict, the Fed is poised to hike. The temporary shutdown of the Saudi East-West pipeline has worsened the energy outlook, and Trump last week levied new tariffs on Canada, adding to existing price pressures. 'The message to the Fed once again is there is no guarantee of anything, especially tariffs, being one-off in the Trump presidency,' CNBC reported.

The vote count within the Federal Open Market Committee is uncertain. At the July meeting, the FOMC voted 9-3 to hold rates steady, with dissenters Lorie Logan of Dallas, Beth Hammack of Cleveland, and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis all supporting a quarter-point hike. To secure a majority for a hike this week, at least four of the nine July hold voters would need to switch sides. Governor Christopher Waller, in remarks on Sept. 3, urged patience, asking, 'What's the cost of waiting one meeting? Hiking 25 basis points, one meeting right now, is not going to bring the [consumer price index] down to 2%.' New York Fed President John Williams also advocated a 'wait-and-see' approach, while Governor Michael Barr said he would be open to a hike. Former New York Fed President Bill Dudley said it 'would be really damaging' to Warsh's credibility if the Fed did nothing, given market expectations.

The vote margin will reveal the depth of the intellectual divide within the Fed over whether inflation is temporary or becoming entrenched, and will signal how effectively Warsh is leading the committee. Some analysts expect that if a majority coalesces around a hike, other members may join to present a united front, potentially yielding only one or two dissents. Markets will also watch the Fed's 'dot plot' update, which will show the anonymous rate expectations of all 19 participants, including the first look at 2029. The Fed almost never hikes or cuts just once, and futures markets are pricing in at least three hikes through March of next year.

The president has publicly harangued the Fed to lower rates, but his own policies have forced the central bank's hand, CNBC reported. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, who dissented in July, wrote that he initially believed the Fed could 'look through' one-time price rises from supply shocks, but now 'increasingly believe[s] that monetary policy does have an important role to play in addressing a series of successive supply shocks that might lead to entrenched higher inflation.' Former Vice Chair Roger Ferguson said on CNBC, 'Everything is pointing in the direction of September as a time to move if Warsh and his colleagues are going to maintain credibility.' The Fed's only job, CNBC noted, is to assess the impact of administration policies on the economy, and given recent developments in Iran and tariffs, 'it would seem difficult for the Fed to assess them as anything but leading to higher inflation in the months ahead.'

stories.headline: China dismisses AI slowdown calls, warns of own AI threats and closing gap with US
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: China on Monday dismissed urgent calls from U.S. tech leaders to slow the development of artificial intelligence, rejecting the warnings as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook” aimed at hobbling Beijing’s progress rather than safeguarding humanity’s future. The response came after a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei — endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk — urged companies to deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their AI models given potential risks. Amodei also warned that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key technology to China.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday. The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.” The comments are the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence. “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”

While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks. State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.” The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington. Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ “Sunday Morning” that the two sides should work together but that he did not hold out much hope. Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”

Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies. Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models. Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies. At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.

China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development. “They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News. “There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion.” Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley. “It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self-restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.

But not everyone is so pessimistic. While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation. “The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said. “You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability. Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

stories.headline: Gates Foundation pledges $1 billion to expand AI access and combat inequality
body: The Gates Foundation, the philanthropic organization backed by Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, pledged on Sept. 15 to spend at least $1 billion globally over the next two years to expand access to artificial intelligence and counter AI-driven inequality. The commitment was announced alongside the release of the foundation's annual Goalkeepers report, which assesses global progress on issues such as ending poverty and reducing inequality. The latest edition highlights the need to ensure AI narrows gaps between the richest and poorest rather than widening them.

The $1 billion pledge is divided across four areas: 40% will go to education, including AI tutoring initiatives; 40% will support healthcare, potentially funding tools for drug and vaccine discovery; 10% will aid agriculture, such as efforts to give smallholder farmers AI-generated advice customized to their soil, weather, and crop conditions; and the remaining 10% will fund projects to build the digital foundation needed for equitable AI access, including incorporating datasets in languages not yet understood by AI tools.

In a video interview on Sept. 11, ahead of the Goalkeepers report launch, Gates Foundation CEO Mark Suzman told The Straits Times that the organization is exploring how more people in Asia, especially those from lower-income and rural areas, could benefit from AI in education, agriculture, and health. He cited the Asia Pathogen Genomics Initiative, established at the Duke-NUS Centre for Outbreak Preparedness in late 2021, as an example of past work at the health-AI nexus. The initiative, now operating in 15 countries, uses an AI-enabled bioinformatics program called PathGen to detect emerging disease threats earlier, assess risks faster, and coordinate responses within and across borders.

The report points to specific examples of AI tools that can benefit underserved populations. It cites MahaVISTAAR, a free AI advisory service for farmers rolled out by the Indian state of Maharashtra, through which farmers can ask questions about crops, weather, and pest management in their own language via an app, voice calls, and chat, receiving verified, localized answers at a cost of less than 18 U.S. cents per farmer. The report also warns of the dangers of mistranslation, noting that a woman in labor in Malawi saying her 'water has broken' in Chichewa could be mistranslated to 'thrown away water' in English, potentially delaying urgent medical advice. It emphasizes that AI tools must be grounded in local data, such as a community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever facing different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital.

Bill Gates, chairman of the foundation, framed the pledge as a response to a market failure. 'The Gates Foundation was created in part to address a basic market failure: The people with the greatest needs often have the least power to shape where innovation and investment go,' he wrote in the report. 'AI presents the same challenge, only at much greater speed. Left to the market alone, the most capable tools will be built first for the people and institutions most able to pay for them – not necessarily for those who could benefit most.' He added, 'We can harness AI for good. But it won't happen by accident. It requires a deliberate, specific commitment from government leaders and the companies developing the technology: to measure success not only by what AI can do for the most profitable users but by what it can do for the people who stand the most to gain.'

Suzman said the foundation is working with partners to ensure AI works in every spoken language, with a focus on languages in Asia and Africa, and may collaborate with the private sector and governments. He noted significant philanthropic resources in Singapore and Malaysia that the foundation could leverage, and said the commitment spans education, agriculture, and health. The foundation said its funding will support partners already working to close AI access gaps and ensure AI tools reflect the knowledge and priorities of those who need them most. The foundation opened its Singapore office in May.
